title.en: Nihongi Book I: The Variant Cosmogonies of the Age of the Gods
title.zh: 日本書紀神代卷創世異傳

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — the celestial scenes of the myth have no earthly location)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:宮崎高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The opening of the Nihongi preserves not one cosmogony but a dossier of them: an official account in which heaven and earth split from a chaotic mass like an egg, and a series of 'In one writing it is said' alternatives in which the first gods spring from a reed-shoot, from floating oil, or from a cloud over the sea, down through seven divine generations to Izanagi and Izanami.
summary.zh: 《日本書紀》開篇並存多種創世說:正文謂天地如雞卵混沌初開,其後又引'一書曰'諸說,謂神自葦芽、浮油或海上雲氣中化生,經神世七代而至伊耶那岐、伊耶那美二神。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I), sacred to Shinto; passages are condensed paraphrases of the public-domain Aston translation, presented for comparative mythology. The Nihongi's variant-listing method reflects the eighth-century court's compilation of rival written sources.

passages.text: Of old, heaven and earth were not yet separated, and the Yin and Yang not yet divided; they formed a chaotic mass like an egg whose limits were ill defined but which contained the germs of all things. The purer and clearer part was thinly drawn out and formed heaven, while the heavier, grosser element settled down and became earth; heaven was therefore formed first and earth established afterwards. Divine beings were then produced between them. The soil of which the lands were composed floated about like a fish sporting on the surface of the water. At that time a thing was produced between heaven and earth in the shape of a reed-shoot, and it became a god, Kuni-toko-tachi no Mikoto. Next came Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto and Toyo-kumu-nu no Mikoto — three deities in all, pure males spontaneously developed by the operation of the principle of heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §1–2 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Nihongi then lets rival traditions speak. In one writing it is said: when heaven and earth began, a thing existed in the midst of the void, its shape beyond description, and within it a deity was spontaneously produced, Kuni-toko-tachi, also called Kuni-soko-tachi; next Kuni no sa-tsuchi, next Toyo-kuni-nushi, who bears many alternate names. In another, when the land was young and floated about like floating oil, a thing shaped like a sprouting reed-shoot was produced within it, and from this was developed the deity Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, next Kuni no toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi. Another says that in the beginning there was first Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji and then Kuni-soko-tachi, no others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §3–5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: A further writing says that when heaven and earth began, deities were produced together — first Kuni-no-toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi — and that in the Plain of High Heaven there were born Ama no mi-naka-nushi, then Taka-mi-musubi, then Kami-mi-musubi. Still another compares the beginning to a cloud floating over the sea, with no place of attachment for its root; from its midst a thing arose resembling a reed-shoot first produced in the mud, which straightway took human shape as Kuni no toko-tachi. Another again has a reed-shoot in the void become the god Ama no toko-tachi, with Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji next, and floating oil in the void from which Kuni-toko-tachi developed. Paired deities followed — Uhiji-ni and Suhiji-ni, Oho-to-nochi and Oho-to-mahe, Omo-taru and Kashiko-ne — until Izanagi and Izanami closed the seven generations of the age of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5–6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The first pages of the Nihongi, Japan's second-oldest written chronicle (720 CE), do something almost no other national myth-cycle does: they preserve a series of competing cosmogonies side by side, introduced by the formula 'In one writing it is said', and let the reader hear each tradition in turn before the narrative proceeds. The opening account, which shows clear Chinese rationalistic influence, describes the original state as a chaotic mass like an egg of obscurely defined limits, containing the germs of all things. The purer, clearer essence spread thinly upward to form heaven, while the heavier, grosser element settled below to become earth — heaven therefore formed first. Between the two, the soil of the future lands floated like a fish sporting on water, and from a thing shaped like a reed-shoot there became manifest the first god, Kuni-toko-tachi no Mikoto, 'Land-Eternal-Stand', followed by Kuni no sa-tsuchi and Toyo-kumu-nu: three nameless, sexless, spontaneously generated deities who represent the bare fact of existence before differentiation.

The 'one writing' alternatives then rework this frame. One says that a thing of indescribable shape existed in the void, and within it a deity spontaneously produced, Kuni-toko-tachi, also called Kuni-soko-tachi; the same text extends the list with Toyo-kuni-nushi, a rich-land-master deity who carries a string of alternate names. Another places the beginning in the land itself, young and drifting like floating oil, and makes the first emergence a thing shaped like a sprouting reed-shoot, from which developed Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, 'Sweet-Reed-Shoot-Prince-Elder', with Kuni no toko-tachi and Kuni no sa-tsuchi after him — a different opening god and a different order. A third, terser, gives only two deities: Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji first, then Kuni-soko-tachi. A fourth locates the first birth not in the void but in the Plain of High Heaven, producing the celestial triad Ama no mi-naka-nushi (the August-Centre-Master of Heaven, whom one commentator identified with the pole star), then Taka-mi-musubi and Kami-mi-musubi, the two growth-gods who dominate later Japanese myth. A fifth imagines a cloud floating over the sea with no root or attachment, from whose midst a reed-shoot-like thing arose and 'straightway became transformed into human shape' as Kuni no toko-tachi — the only variant that stresses immediate anthropomorphism. A sixth gives Ama no toko-tachi, 'Heaven-Eternal-Stand', as the first god, with Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji following, and adds floating oil from which Kuni-toko-tachi developed.

After the variants, the text resumes a common thread: paired deities come into being — Uhiji-ni and Suhiji-ni (mud-earth and sand-earth), Oho-to-nochi and Oho-to-mahe, Omo-taru and Kashiko-ne — until the series culminates in the male and female pair Izanagi and Izanami. This line of seven generations, from Kuni no toko-tachi through the mating pairs to Izanagi and Izanami, is what the tradition calls the seven generations of the age of the gods. One appended writing even offers a chain in which Kuni no toko-tachi produced Ame-kagami, who produced Ame-yorodzu, who produced Aha-nagi, who produced Izanagi — eight deities formed by the mutual action of the heavenly and earthly principles.

The cultural function of this dossier is twofold. Politically, it anchors the imperial line in an unbroken divine genealogy: the eighth-century court needed the gods that precede the creation of Japan to be ordered, named, and countable, so that the descent of the imperial ancestors from them could be certified. Theologically and comparatively, it shows the compilers' honesty about the plurality of tradition: the same corpus that asserts one official cosmogony also archives five or six rivals. Some of the variants bear the stamp of imported Chinese philosophy (the Yin-Yang egg, the paired 'principles of heaven and earth'); others look like older native germination-myths, in which life sprouts like a reed in mud. The figure of the reed-shoot links this Japanese material to the wider cluster of creation-from-chaos myths — the dismembered primordial bodies of Ymir or Pangu, or the watery chaos of Babylonian Tiamat — though here nothing violent happens: the world differentiates by settling and sprouting, not by combat. The variant list was quarried for centuries by Shinto theologians, who used the abundance of names either to harmonize the sources or to defend the orthodox Kuni-toko-tachi-centered sequence of later state Shinto.

functions: Legitimates the imperial dynasty by anchoring it in a certified seven-generation divine genealogy.
Exposes the Nihongi's court-compilation method: Chinese-style cosmological framing set beside older native sprouting-myths.
Provides the deity-list (Kuni-toko-tachi, Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji, the Musubi gods) used by Shinto ritual and by later theologians to harmonize rival traditions.
Explains the origin of the land as spontaneous differentiation of a chaotic egg-like mass rather than through combat.
