title.en: Nihongi Variant: Izanagi and Izanami Create the Island of Onogoro
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·伊耶那岐神與伊耶那美神造淤能碁呂島

region.en: Onogoro / Awaji (symbolic pin between Awaji Island and the Inland Sea)
region.zh: 淤能碁呂島/淡路島(象徵定位)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Izanagi and Izanami stand on the floating bridge of heaven, stir the ocean with the jewel-spear of heaven, and the dripping brine congeals into the island of Onogoro. Circling the central pillar, the couple marries — but the woman speaks first, an omen of ill luck, and the Nihongi preserves several variant accounts of how the islands of Japan were produced and ordered.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐、伊耶那美二神立於天上浮橋,以天沼矛攪動滄海,滴落之鹽凝成淤能碁呂島。二神繞國中之柱成婚,因女子先發言而遭不祥;書紀並存多種島嶼誕生順序的異傳。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Izanagi and Izanami stood on the floating bridge of heaven and held counsel: was there not a country beneath? They thrust down the jewel-spear of heaven and groped about therewith until they found the ocean; the brine dripping from the point coagulated and became the island Onogoro-jima. Descending, the two deities wished to become husband and wife and to produce countries, and made Onogoro the pillar of the centre of the land. The male deity, turning by the left, and the female deity by the right, went round the pillar separately; when they met, the female spoke first — 'How delightful! I have met with a lovely youth!' The male was displeased: by right he, a man, should have spoken first; this was unlucky. They went round again, and this time the male spoke first: 'How delightful! I have met a lovely maiden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asked the female deity whether in her body there was aught formed; she said there was a place which was the source of femineity. He answered that his body had a place which was the source of masculinity, and he wished to unite the two. So they became husband and wife. When the time of birth came, the island of Ahaji was first reckoned as the placenta, and their minds took no pleasure in it, so it was named the island which will not meet. Next they produced Oho-yamato-toyo-aki-tsu-shima, then Iyo and Tsukushi; Oki and Sado were born as twins, the prototype of twin-births among mankind; then Koshi, Oho-shima and Kibi no Ko — hence the name Great-Eight-Island country — while Tsushima, Iki and the small islands congealed from the foam of the salt water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §5–6 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In one writing it is said: the Gods of heaven addressed Izanagi and Izanami — there is the floating country Toyo-ashi-hara-chi-i-wo-aki no midzu-ho; do ye proceed and bring it into order — and gave them the jewel-spear of heaven. The two gods stood on the floating bridge, plunged the spear down and stirred the ocean; the dripping brine coagulated into Onogoro, where they descended, dwelt, erected an eight-fathom palace, and set up the pillar of heaven. Their first child was the leech, whom they placed in a reed-boat and sent adrift; next was Ahaji, also not counted among their children. They returned to heaven and made report; the Heavenly Gods divined and instructed them that the woman's having spoken first was the cause, so they went round the pillar again, the male this time from the left, and thereafter had children who were the islands of Japan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §6–7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Still other writings vary the quest for land. The two deities stood in the midst of the mist of heaven, wished to find a country, thrust down the spear and found Onogoro, drawing it back with joy: 'Good! there is a country!' In another they sat in the Plain of High Heaven and scraped the island together with the spear; in another, seeing something resembling floating oil, they suspected a country in its midst and formed the island by groping with the spear. One curious writing relates that after the female deity spoke first and they went round again, the couple longed to unite but knew not the art, until a wagtail flew up, shook its head and its tail, and the two gods imitated the bird and so obtained the art of union. The order of the islands also varies from writing to writing, with Ahaji, Onogoro or Aha variously named as the placenta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §7–8 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: The Birth of the Sun, the Moon and the Leech Child
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·日月誕生與水蛭子

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — celestial scenes)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Having made the islands, mountains and trees, Izanagi and Izanami ask who shall be lord of the universe and produce the resplendent Sun-Goddess Oho-hiru-me, then the Moon-god, then the leech child who cannot stand, and finally the violent Susanoo, whom they expel to the Nether Land. Variant writings make the sun and moon born from Izanagi's copper mirrors, and reorder the leech child's place in the sequence.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐、伊耶那美造國既畢,欲生治理天下之貴子,遂生大日孁貴(天照大神)、月神,復生不能站立之水蛭子,及性情暴戾之素戔嗚尊,其父母逐之往根國。一書另謂日月自伊耶那岐手中白銅鏡化生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After producing the sea, the rivers and the mountains, and the ancestors of trees and herbs, Izanagi and Izanami consulted together: they had produced the Great-Eight-Island country with its mountains, rivers, herbs and trees — why not now produce someone who should be lord of the universe? So they together produced the Sun-Goddess, Oho-hiru-me no muchi, whose resplendent lustre shone through all six quarters. Rejoicing, the parents said that though they had many children, none equalled this wondrous infant; she ought not to be kept long in this land, so they sent her up to heaven by the ladder of heaven to be entrusted with the affairs of heaven. Next they produced the Moon-god, Tsuki-yumi, whose radiance was next to the sun's; he was to be the Sun-Goddess's consort and share her government, and him also they sent up to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next they produced the leech child, which even at three years of age could not stand upright; they placed it in the rock-camphor-wood boat of heaven and abandoned it to the winds. Their next child was Sosa no wo (Susanoo), of fierce temper and given to cruel acts, continually weeping and wailing, bringing many people of the land to untimely death and withering the green mountains. His parents therefore addressed him: it was not meet that he should reign over the world; he must depart far away to the Nether Land — and at length they expelled him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §16–17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In one writing it is said: Izanagi declared that he wished to procreate the precious child who was to rule the world. He took a white-copper mirror in his left hand, and a deity was produced from it, Oho-hiru-me; a mirror in his right hand produced Tsuki-yumi; and while turning his head and looking askance, a god was produced who was Sosa no wo. The two mirror-born deities were bright and beautiful in nature and were made to shine down on heaven and earth, but Susanoo's nature was to love destruction, so he was sent down to rule the Nether Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §17 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another writing places the leech child after the sun and moon, and explains his deformity: because, when the parents first went round the pillar, the female deity was the first to utter a cry of pleasure, the law of male and female was broken. This Susanoo was of a wicked nature, always fond of wailing and wrath, so that many of the people died and the green mountains withered; his parents told him he must govern the far-distant Nether Land. Their next child, in this version, was the bird-rock-camphor-wood boat of heaven, in which they placed the leech child and abandoned it to the current; their next child was Kagutsuchi, the fire god, by whom his mother Izanami was burnt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §18–19 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variants: Kagutsuchi the Fire God and the Death of Izanami
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·火之迦具土神與伊耶那美之死

region.en: Arima in Kumano, Kii province (burial place of Izanami in one variant; modern Kumano district, Kii Peninsula)
region.zh: 紀伊國熊野有馬村(異傳中伊耶那美葬地)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: When the fire god Kagutsuchi is born, his mother Izanami is burnt and dies; on her deathbed she brings forth the water and earth goddesses, and in one startling variant from her vomit, urine and excrement. Izanagi in grief cuts Kagutsuchi into three or five pieces, which become thunder, mountains and rock-gods, while the blood on his sword becomes deities in the bed of the Milky Way; one variant tells of an annual flower festival still held at Izanami's grave in Kumano.
summary.zh: 火神迦具土誕生時燒傷其母伊耶那美,母臨終生水神、土神;一書更謂其吐物、尿、糞亦化為神。伊耶那岐悲痛,拔劍斬迦具土為三段或五段,化為雷神、山神等;血濺劍刃化為神,草木瓦石遂含火性。一書謂伊耶那美葬於熊野有馬村,其地民間以花祭祀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Izanami gave birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi she was burnt by the child and died. As she lay dying she gave birth to the earth goddess Hani-yama-hime and the water goddess Midzu-ha-no-me. Kagutsuchi then took Hani-yama-hime to wife, and they had a child, Waka-musubi, on whose head were produced the silkworm and the mulberry tree, and in whose navel the five kinds of grain — a tradition which betrays a comparatively recent origin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §19–20 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Other writings embroider the death. In one, when Izanami was about to die she brought forth, besides the water and earth goddesses, the gourd of heaven, to hold water for subduing the fire god when he grew violent. In another, at the birth Kagutsuchi made her feverish and ill: she vomited, and the vomit became the metal-mountain god Kana-yama-hiko; her urine became the water goddess Midzu-ha-no-me; her excrement became the clay goddess Hani-yama-hime. A third adds that Izanami was buried at the village of Arima in Kumano in Kii, where the inhabitants worship her spirit with offerings of flowers in the time of flowers, and with drums, flutes, flags, singing and dancing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §20–21 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Izanagi was wroth, lamenting that he had given his beloved younger sister in exchange for a single child, and crawled at her head and feet weeping; the tears became the deity Naki-saha-me, weeping-abundant-female, who dwells at Unewo no Konomoto. At length he drew the ten-span sword at his girdle and cut Kagutsuchi into three pieces, each of which became a god. The blood dripping from the sword's edge became the multitudinous rocks in the bed of the Easy River of heaven — the Milky Way; the blood from the hilt-ring spurted out and became deities, among them the ancestor of Take-mika-dzuchi; the blood from the point became Iha-saku, Ne-saku and Iha-tsutsu-wo, the father of Futsu-nushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §22–23 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another writing has him cut Kagutsuchi into five pieces, which became the five mountain gods: the head became Oho-yama-tsu-mi, the trunk Naka-yama-tsu-mi, the hands Ha-yama-tsu-mi, the loins Masa-katsu-yama-tsu-mi, and the feet Shiki-yama-tsu-mi. At that time the blood from the wounds spurted out and stained the rocks, trees and herbage: this is the reason that herbs, trees and pebbles naturally contain the element of fire — an etiology of how fire lies dormant in all growing and mineral things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §24 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Izanagi's Flight from Yomi, the Land of the Dead
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·伊耶那岐神逃出黃泉國

region.en: Yomi, the Even Pass of Yomi (symbolic inland pin)
region.zh: 黃泉國、黃泉比良坂(象徵內陸定位)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Izanagi follows his dead wife into Yomi, breaks the taboo against looking at her by torchlight, and flees as she swarms with maggots and thunder-gods. He flings down grapes, bamboo shoots and a peach, blocks the Even Pass with a great rock, and pronounces the formula of divorce; Izanami threatens to kill a thousand people a day and he answers he will cause fifteen hundred to be born. The Nihongi's telling adds details absent from the Kojiki: the spitting purification, the council of Kukuri-hime, and the superstitions about single lights and discarded combs.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐入黃泉尋妻,違禁以火照視,見妻屍腐爛生蟲,倉皇逃歸。黃泉醜女追之,他投葡萄、筍與桃以阻之,以大石塞黃泉坂,並誦絕婚之辭;伊耶那美揚言日殺千人,他答日生千五百人。書紀此異傳增入吐唾祓除、菊理姬調停及夜間忌單燈、忌棄梳等俗信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Thereafter Izanagi went after Izanami and entered the land of Yomi. She asked why his coming was so late: she had already eaten of the cooking-furnace of Yomi, yet she was about to lie down to rest — do not look on me. He did not give ear, but secretly took his many-toothed comb, broke off its end tooth for a torch, and looked at her: putrefying matter had gushed up and maggots swarmed. This, the text says, is why people still avoid using a single light at night, and avoid throwing away a comb at night. Shocked, Izanagi cried that he had come unawares to a hideous and polluted land, and ran away; Izanami, shamed and angry, sent the eight Ugly Females of Yomi to pursue and stay him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §24 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Izanagi drew his sword, flourished it behind him, and flung down his black head-dress, which became grapes the Ugly Females ate before resuming the chase. He flung his comb, which became bamboo shoots, which they pulled up and ate — and still they pursued. Then Izanami herself came after him. According to one account, he made water against a great tree, and the water turned at once into a great river; while the Ugly Females prepared to cross it, he reached the Even Pass of Yomi, took a thousand-men-pull rock, blocked the path, stood face to face with Izanami and pronounced the formula of divorce. She replied that if he said so, she would strangle a thousand of the people of his country in one day; he answered that then he would cause fifteen hundred to be born in one day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §25–26 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Come no further, he said, and threw down his staff, which was called Funado; then his girdle, which became Naga-chi-ha; his upper garment, Wadzurahi; his trowsers, Aki-gui; and his shoes, Chi-shiki. In one variant, as Izanagi fled from the eight thunders resting on the swollen and festering corpse of Izanami, a great peach tree grew by the roadside; he concealed himself at its foot and flung its fruit at the thunders, which all ran away — the origin of the practice of keeping off evil spirits by means of peaches.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §26–28 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: In another writing, when Izanagi declared their relationship severed — I will not submit to be beaten by a relation — he spat, and the God of his spittle was Haya-tama no wo, with Yomo-tsu-koto-saka no wo as the god of his purification. The Road-wardens of Yomi brought a message: the two had produced countries together, and she would stay in this land; at this Kukuri-hime said something which Izanagi heard and approved, and she vanished away. Some say the Even Pass of Yomi is no particular place, but only the space of time when the breath fails at the approach of death; the blocking rock was worshipped as the Yomi-gate-block deity, also called the Road-turn-back Great God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §29 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Izanagi's Purification at Wodo in Hiuga
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·日向橘小戶阿波岐原之禊

region.en: Wodo (Ahagi plain) in Hiuga, Tsukushi — modern Hyuga, Miyazaki
region.zh: 日向國橘小戶阿波岐原(今宮崎縣日向市)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Returning from the pollution of Yomi, Izanagi washes in the sea at Ahagi plain in Wodo, Hiuga. Washing away his body's ills, then plunging bottom, mid-tide and surface, he produces three successive companies of gods; finally, washing his left eye, right eye and nose, he produces Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo and assigns their realms. Variant writings give a different scheme of deities born from entering and leaving the water, and a different division of the three children's charges.
summary.zh: 伊耶那岐自黃泉歸,謂須祓除穢氣,遂至日向橘小戶阿波岐原,於中流洗滌;滌罪、入海洗、洗面部,各生諸神;最後洗左眼生天照大神、右眼生月讀尊、洗鼻生素戔嗚尊,分授職司。一書所生神名及三子職分均異。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); the misogi purification is the ritual charter of Shinto ablution; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Izanagi had returned he was seized with regret: having gone to a hideous and filthy place, it was meet that he should cleanse his body from its pollutions. He went to the plain of Ahagi at Tachibana in Wodo in Hiuga of Tsukushi and purified himself. About to wash away the impurities of his body, he lifted up his voice and said that the upper stream was too rapid and the lower too sluggish, so he would wash in the middle stream; the god thereby produced was Ya-so-maga-tsu-bi, and to remedy these evils were produced Kami-nawo-bi and Oho-nawo-bi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §26–27 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Deities were also produced by his plunging down and washing in the bottom of the sea — Soko-tsu-wata-tsu-mi and Soko-tsutsu-wo; by washing in the mid-tide — Naka-tsu-wata-dzu-mi and Naka-tsutsu-wo; and by washing floating on the surface — Uha-tsu-wata-dzu-mi and Uha-tsutsu-wo, nine gods in all, including the three great gods of Suminoye and the gods worshipped by the Muraji of Adzumi. Thereafter, washing his left eye he produced Ama-terasu, his right eye Tsuki-yomi, and his nose Sosa no wo; to them he gave charge: Amaterasu to rule the plain of High Heaven, Tsuki-yomi the eight-hundred-fold tides of the ocean plain, and Susanoo to rule the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §27–28 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: A variant writing gives a different scheme: visiting the Aha gate and the Haya-sufu-na gate to purify himself, he found the tide too strong, so he returned to Wodo in Tachibana. Entering the water he blew out and produced Iha-tsu-tsu, and coming out of the water blew forth Oho-nawo-bi; entering a second time he produced Soko-tsutsu and, coming out, Oho-aya-tsu-bi; entering again he produced Aka-tsutsu, and coming out he blew forth the various deities of heaven, of earth and of the sea-plain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §30 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another writing alters even the charge to the three children: Amaterasu to rule the plain of High Heaven, Tsuki-yomi to be associated with her in heavenly matters, and Susanoo to govern the plain of ocean. At this time Susanoo was already of full age, with a beard eight spans long, yet he neglected to rule the world, always weeping, wailing and raging; asked why, he answered that he wished to follow his mother to the Nether Land. Izanagi, filled with detestation, told him to go as his heart bade him, and drove him away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §29 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Tsukuyomi Slays the Food Goddess Ukemochi
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·月讀尊殺保食神

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — celestial scenes)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Amaterasu sends the Moon-god Tsukuyomi to the food goddess Ukemochi, who regurgitates rice, fish and game from her mouth to feast him. Disgusted, he draws his sword and slays her, and for this the Sun and Moon are separated to dwell apart, one by day and one by night. From the slain goddess's corpse come the ox, horse, silkworm and the five grains, which Amaterasu sows — the origin of agriculture and sericulture.
summary.zh: 天照大神遣月讀尊往侍保食神。保食神面向陸海山原,自口吐飯食魚獸待客;月讀尊怒其穢,拔劍殺之。天照大神因此與月讀尊晝夜分離,不得相見。後使者於其屍上得牛馬、蠶桑、五穀,天照大神播種於天上田畝,養蠶繅絲,遂有農桑之始。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Amaterasu, already in heaven, heard that in the Central Country of reed-plains dwelt the deity Uke-mochi, the goddess of food. She sent Tsuki-yomi to wait upon her. Uke-mochi turned her head towards the land, and boiled rice came from her mouth; she faced the sea, and things broad of fin and narrow of fin came from her mouth; she faced the mountains, and things rough of hair and soft of hair came from her mouth. All these were prepared and set out on one hundred tables for his entertainment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tsuki-yomi flushed with anger: 'Filthy! Nasty! That thou shouldst dare to feed me with things disgorged from thy mouth!' So he drew his sword and slew her, then returned and made his report. Amaterasu was exceedingly angry: 'Thou art a wicked deity. I must not see thee face to face.' So they were separated by one day and one night, and dwelt apart — the Nihongi's explanation of why sun and moon are never seen together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards Amaterasu sent Ame-kuma-bito to see the goddess again. She was truly dead already, but on the crown of her head had been produced the ox and the horse; on her forehead, millet; over her eyebrows, the silkworm; within her eyes, panic; in her belly, rice; in her genitals, wheat, large beans and small beans. Amaterasu rejoiced: these were the things by which the race of visible men would eat and live. She made the millet, panic, wheat and beans seed for the dry fields, and rice the seed for the water-fields; she appointed a village-chief of heaven and sowed the rice seed for the first time in the narrow and long fields of heaven. That autumn drooping ears bent down, eight spans long, pleasant to look upon. She took the silkworms in her mouth and reeled thread from them — from this began the art of silkworm rearing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §32–33 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Susanoo's Oath with Amaterasu at the True Wells of Heaven
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·須佐之男命與天照大神之盟誓

region.en: Plain of High Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki — celestial scenes)
region.zh: 高天原(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Susanoo, about to descend to the Nether Land, forces his way up to heaven to see his sister. Amaterasu dons male war-gear and challenges him; to prove the purity of his heart he proposes an oath in which each chews the other's sword or jewels, and the children born prove innocence if male, guilt if female. From her sword come three Munakata goddesses, from his jewels five male gods. Several rival writings rearrange the oath, the wells, the gifts and the children's parentage.
summary.zh: 素戔嗚尊欲往根國,強登高天原面見其姊。天照大神易男裝執弓矢,詰問其來意。為自證清白,二神於天真井旁盟誓:互相咀嚼對方之劍與勾玉而生子,生男則心清白,生女則心邪穢。天照大神嚼劍生三女神(市杵島姬等,即宗像三神),素戔嗚尊嚼勾玉生五男神。書紀並存數種誓約異傳。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Susanoo went up to heaven, the fierceness of his divine nature made the sea commotion and the hills and mountains groan aloud. Amaterasu, knowing his violence, was startled: he must mean to rob her of her kingdom, rejecting the realm to which his parents had assigned him. She bound up her hair in knots and tied her skirts into the form of trowsers, entwined a string of five hundred Yasaka jewels around her hair and wrists, slung a thousand-arrow and a five-hundred-arrow quiver on her back, drew on a dread loud-sounding elbow-pad, brandished her bow and grasped her sword-hilt, stamping the hard earth of the courtyard as if it were foam-snow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §35 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having uttered a mighty cry of defiance, she questioned him. Susanoo answered that his heart had never been black: obeying the stern behest of their parents, he was departing for ever to the Nether Land, and could not bear to go without seeing her face to face; he was surprised she wore so stern a countenance. Asked how he would make evident the redness of his heart, he proposed they swear an oath together and produce children: if the children he produced were females, his heart was impure; if males, pure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §35 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu took Susanoo's ten-span sword, broke it into three pieces, rinsed them in the true-well of heaven, chewed them with a crunching noise and blew them away; from the mist of her breath were born three goddesses, Ta-gori-bime, Tagi-tsu-bime and Ichiki-shima-bime — deities worshipped by the Munagata no Kimi of Tsukushi. Susanoo in turn begged her string of five hundred Yasaka jewels, rinsed it in the true-well, chewed it and blew it away; from his breath came five male gods, the first named Masa-ya-a-katsu-kachi-hayabi-ama no oshi-ho-mimi. She claimed the five males as her children, since their seed was her necklace, and gave the three females to Susanoo as his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §36 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Rival writings rearrange the rite. In one, the goddess stands on the further side of the Tranquil River of heaven and swears that if his heart is pure the children will be males; she eats first a ten-span, then a nine-span, then an eight-span sword, producing the three goddesses; Susanoo chews his five-hundred-jewel string from the left knot of his hair and produces six males, whom she takes to govern the Plain of Heaven. In another they dig three true wells and exchange sword for jewels before chewing them; in a third, a deity Ha-akaru-tama meets Susanoo and gives him maga-tama of Yasaka jewels to present to his sister, with which he proves his innocence and departs for ever to the Nether Land, delivering his children to her keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §37–40 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Amaterasu Hides in the Rock Cave of Heaven
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·天照大神閉居天石屋

region.en: Rock Cave of Heaven (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki)
region.zh: 天石屋戶(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Susanoo ravages his sister's rice-fields and flays a heavenly piebald colt in her sacred weaving hall, so that Amaterasu, wounded and alarmed, shuts herself in the Rock Cave of Heaven and the world falls into constant darkness. The eight-hundred-myriad gods gather by the Tranquil River, make offerings, and Ama no Uzume performs a divinely inspired dance until the goddess peeps out; Tajikara-wo pulls her into the light, the gods draw a bottom-tied rope across the cave mouth, and Susanoo is fined a thousand tables and banished. Variant writings tell the offence differently and even have the goddess die in the weaving hall.
summary.zh: 素戔嗚尊毀天照大神之田溝,放天斑駒於田中,於新宮穢處,復於神織殿剝皮投駒。天照大神驚懼,以梭傷身,遂閉天石屋戶,天下常暗。八百萬神集於天安河原,思金神設謀,天兒屋命、布刀玉命供神饌,天鈿女命執矛而舞,神靈感之;天照大神窺探,手力雄神引之出,以注連繩橫絕其歸路。眾神課素戔嗚尊千座贖罪物,拔其鬚眉爪甲,終逐之下界。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Amaterasu had made heavenly narrow and heavenly long rice-fields; Susanoo, when the seed was sown in spring, broke down the divisions between the plots, and in autumn let loose the heavenly piebald colts to lie down in the midst of the rice-fields. When she was about to celebrate the feast of first-fruits he secretly voided excrement in the New Palace; and when she was in her sacred weaving hall weaving the garments of the gods, he flayed a piebald colt of heaven and, breaking a hole in the roof-tiles, flung it in. She started with alarm and wounded herself with the shuttle; indignant, she straightway entered the Rock Cave of Heaven and fastened the Rock-door. Constant darkness prevailed on all sides, and the alternation of night and day was unknown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §40 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The eighty-myriad gods met on the bank of the Tranquil River of heaven to consider how to supplicate her. Omohi-kane, with profound device, gathered long-singing birds of the Eternal Land to utter their prolonged cry to one another, and set Tajikara-wo, Hand-Strength-Male, beside the Rock-door. Ame no Koyane, ancestor of the Nakatomi, and Futo-dama, ancestor of the Imibe, dug up a five-hundred-branched true Sakaki tree of the heavenly Mount Kagu: on its upper branches they hung a string of five hundred Yasaka jewels, on the middle branches the eight-hand mirror, on the lower branches blue and white soft offerings, and recited their liturgy together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §41–42 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ama no Uzume, ancestress of the Sarume, took a spear wreathed with Eulalia grass, stood before the door of the Rock Cave, and skilfully performed a mimic dance; she made a head-dress of true Sakaki, braces of club-moss, kindled fires, placed a tub bottom upwards and gave forth a divinely-inspired utterance. Amaterasu heard her and wondered how she could be so jolly while the world sat in darkness; she opened the Rock-door a narrow space and peeped out. Tajikara-wo forthwith took her by the hand and led her out; the Nakatomi and Imibe gods drew a limit with a bottom-tied, left-hand rope and begged her not to return into the cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §42 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gods blamed Susanoo, imposed on him a fine of one thousand tables, plucked out his hair to make him expiate his guilt — in one version, the nails of his hands and feet — and banished him downwards. In one writing the offender is punished in a different currency: of his finger-nail parings they made the things abhorrent of luck, of his toe-nails the things abhorrent of calamity, and of his spittle and nose-mucus they made the blue and white offerings with which the purification service was performed. Another variant has Waka-hiru-me, a younger sister of the Sun-Goddess, die of her wound in the weaving hall, and an image of her made by Ishi-kori-dome out of copper with heavenly bellows — the goddess Hi no mahe who dwells in Kii. In yet another, the mirror made for the cave struck the Rock-door and received a slight flaw which remains to this day — the great deity worshipped at Ise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §43–45 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variants: Susanoo and the Eight-Forked Serpent
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·須佐之男命斬八岐大蛇

region.en: Upper waters of the River Hi, Izumo

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Banished from heaven, Susanoo descends to the head-waters of the River Hi in Izumo, where an elderly couple weep for their last daughter, doomed to be devoured by an eight-forked serpent. He turns the girl into a comb, has her parents brew eight-fold sake, and, when the monster has drunk itself asleep, hacks it apart and finds the sword Kusanagi in its tail. Variant writings relocate the fight, rename the swords, and send Susanoo via Silla — where his son plants the seeds of all the trees of Japan and his body-hairs become cryptomerias and camphors.
summary.zh: 素戔嗚尊既遭逐,降於出雲肥河上流,遇足名椎、手名椎夫婦哭其幼女櫛名田比賣,言八岐大蛇歲年食其女。素戔嗚尊化女為梳,令釀八醞之酒,蛇來各飲一器,醉而眠;遂拔十拳劍碎斬之,於尾中得草薙劍(一名天叢雲劍),奉上天。一書改言毒酒、劍名、地點;又一書謂素戔嗚尊攜子五十猛命經新羅渡來,播種樹木,毛髮化為杉、檜、樟等,終登熊成峰而入根國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Susanoo descended from heaven to the head-waters of the River Hi in Izumo, where he heard the sound of weeping and found an old man and an old woman caressing a young girl between them. They were earthly deities, Ashi-nadzuchi and Te-nadzuchi; the girl was their daughter Kushi-nada-hime, and they grieved because an eight-forked serpent had devoured their eight daughters year after year, and the time drew near for her to be devoured. Susanoo asked for her hand, changed her into a many-toothed close-comb which he stuck in his hair, and had her parents brew eight-fold sake and set a tub in each of eight cupboards to await the serpent's coming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §44 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The serpent appeared, with an eight-forked head and an eight-forked tail; its eyes were red like the winter-cherry, and on its back firs and cypresses were growing; as it crawled it extended over eight hills and eight valleys. Each head drank up one tub and it became drunken and fell asleep. Susanoo drew his ten-span sword and chopped the serpent into small pieces; when he came to the tail, the edge of the sword was slightly notched, so he split it open and found within it a sword. This is the sword called Kusa-nagi no tsurugi — originally, one writing says, Ama no Mura-kumo, the sword of the gathering clouds of heaven. Susanoo said: this is a divine sword; how can I presume to appropriate it? So he gave it up to the gods of heaven, built a palace at Suga, where his heart was refreshed, composed the first Japanese poem on its manifold fences, and begot on Kushi-nada-hime the god Oho-na-muchi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §44–45 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Other writings vary the details. In one, the parents themselves instruct Susanoo to brew eight jars of sake from fruit of all kinds; he addresses the serpent with feigned reverence, pours one jar into each of its mouths, and kills it; the sword that slew it is called Worochi no Kara-masa and is kept at Isonokami, while the sword found in the tail, Kusa-nagi, rests with the Hafuri of Atsuta. Another makes the sake poisonous; in yet another, Susanoo, fined a thousand tables by the gods and banished, first goes with his son Iso-takeru to the land of Silla, dwells at Soshi-mori, refuses to stay, makes a boat of clay, and crosses eastwards to Mount Tori-kamu in Izumo, where with the sword Ama no Haye-kiri he slays another man-devouring serpent and finds the divine sword in its tail, sending it up to heaven by his descendant in the fifth generation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §46–47 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The same writing continues with an etiology of Japan's forests: Iso-takeru, descending from heaven, carried tree seeds in great quantity; he did not plant them in the land of Han but brought them all back and sowed them throughout the Great Eight-Island country, beginning with Tsukushi — thus the green mountains were produced, and he was styled Isaoshi, the Meritorious God, dwelling in the land of Kii. His father, resolving that his son's country should not lack floating riches, plucked out his beard and scattered it, and cryptomerias were produced; the hairs of his breast became thuyas, of his buttocks podocarps, of his eyebrows camphor-trees, each assigned its use — ships, palace timber, burial receptacles. With his daughters Iso-takeru, Oho-ya-tsu-hime and Tsuma-tsu-hime, who dispersed the seeds and crossed to Kii, Susanoo dwelt at last on the Peak of Kuma-nari and eventually entered the Nether Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §47–48 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: Okuninushi and Sukunabikona Make the World Whole
title.zh: 日本書紀·大己貴神與少名毘古那神修治國土

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Oho-na-mochi (Okuninushi), lord of one hundred and eighty-one divine children and bearer of many names, and the tiny deity Sukunabikona, with united strength and one heart, construct the sub-celestial world, determine the healing of diseases, and devise means against the calamities of birds, beasts and creeping things. When Sukunabikona departs to the Everlasting Land, Okuninushi finishes the work alone; a divine radiance reveals his guardian spirit, who is enshrined on Mount Mimoro as the god of Oho-miwa. A second episode tells how the dwarf-god arrived from over the sea in a boat of kagami rind, dressed in wren feathers.
summary.zh: 大己貴神(大國主神)多別名,有一百八十一子之神;與少名毘古那神同心協力,造作幽顯之國,定療病之方,并治鳥獸蟲豸之災。少名毘古那神後渡常世國去,大己貴神獨自巡治未備之地,於出雲自言平國之功。時神光照海,其守護之神(幸魂奇魂)現,願居大和三輪山,遂建神宮,是為大三輪之神。又一書詳載少名毘古那神自海上乘神鏡果皮之舟、著鷦鷯羽衣而來之事。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Oho-kuni-nushi, also called Oho-mono-nushi, Kuni-dzukuri Oho-na-mochi, Ashi-hara no Shiko-wo, Ya-chi-hoko, Oho-kuni-dama and Utsushi-kuni-dama, had one hundred and eighty-one children. Now Oho-na-mochi and Sukuna-bikona, with united strength and one heart, constructed this sub-celestial world; then, for the sake of the visible race of man as well as of beasts, they determined the method of healing diseases, and, to do away with the calamities of birds, beasts and creeping things, established means for their prevention and control. The people enjoy the protection of these universally to the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §50 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before this, Oho-na-mochi had asked Sukuna-bikona whether the country they had made were well made; the dwarf answered that in some parts it was complete and in others incomplete — a conversation of mysterious purport. Thereafter Sukuna-bikona went to Cape Kumano and eventually proceeded to the Everlasting Land; another version says he went to the island of Aha, climbed up a millet-stalk, was jerked off, and so departed. Wherever the land was imperfect, Oho-na-mochi visited it himself and repaired it, coming at last to Izumo, where he declared that the Central Land of Reed-plains, always waste and wild — its very rocks, trees and herbs given to violence — had been reduced by him to submission, and that he alone now governed the land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §50–51 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he asked who could join him in governing the world, a divine radiance illuminated the sea, and something suddenly floated towards him and said: were I not here, how couldst thou subdue this land? It is because I am here that thou hast accomplished this mighty undertaking. Asked who he was, the spirit replied that he was his guardian spirit, the wondrous spirit. Oho-na-mochi acknowledged him, and the spirit answered that he wished to dwell on Mount Mimoro in Yamato; accordingly Okuninushi built a shrine there for him. This is the God of Oho-miwa — whose children, one version says, include Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime, who became the consort of Emperor Kami-yamato-ihare-biko; for in that account Koto-shiro-nushi, transformed into an eight-fathom bear-sea-monster, had union with Mizo-kuhi-hime of the island of Mishima.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §51–52 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another episode explains the dwarf's origin. When Oho-na-mochi was pacifying the land, eating and drinking at Wobama in Isasa in Izumo, a human voice was suddenly heard from the surface of the sea, though nothing could be seen. After a while a dwarf appeared, who had made a boat of the rind of a kagami and clothing of the feathers of a wren, and came floating on the tide. Oho-na-mochi took him up on the palm of his hand and played with him, until the dwarf leaped up and bit him on the cheek. Astonished, Okuninushi sent a messenger to report to the gods of heaven, and Taka-mi-musubi replied that among his fifteen hundred children was one wicked child who would not yield compliance and had slipped through his fingers: this must be that child — let him be loved and nurtured. This was Sukuna-bikona himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §52–53 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·伊耶那岐神幽居

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The Nihongi gives Izanagi two competing deaths. After his divine task is accomplished and his spirit-career about to change, he builds an abode of gloom on the island of Ahaji and dwells there for ever in silence and concealment; another account has him ascend to heaven, report his mission, and take up residence in the smaller palace of the Sun. These variants stand where the Kojiki places the god's death and burial on Mount Taga.
summary.zh: 《日本書紀》所載伊耶那岐神之終局有二說:一謂其神功既畢,於淡道島作幽宮,隱而終身不復出;一謂其登天復命,居日之小宮。此與《古事記》伊耶那岐神葬於多賀之說相對應。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book I); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After this, Izanagi the creator god reached the end of his long career. His divine task having been accomplished and his spirit-career about to suffer a change, he built himself an abode of gloom in the island of Ahaji, where he dwelt for ever in silence and concealment, hidden from the sight of gods and men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §33 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another account says that Izanagi, his task having been accomplished and his power great, ascended to heaven and made report of his mission; there he dwelt in the smaller palace of the Sun — by smaller palace being meant the palace of a prince. The Nihongi thus closes the creator god's story with two alternative endings, a hidden death in the island where his first unwanted island-birth had served as placenta, or a retired residence in the Sun's own court, while the Kojiki honours his grave at Taga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book I §33 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: The Failed Envoy Ame-waka-hiko and the Origin of the Funeral Dirge
title.zh: 日本書紀·天稚彥之死與鳥葬悲歌

region.en: Plain of High Heaven and the Central Land of Reed-Plains (symbolic pin on the Takachiho plateau for the celestial scenes)
region.zh: 高天原與葦原中國(象徵定位:高千穗高原)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Sent from heaven to subdue the Central Land of Reed-Plains, Ame-waka-hiko disobeys, marries an earthly deity's daughter, and never reports. When the pheasant spy Na-naki is shot, the arrow returns to heaven and is flung back to pierce him at the feast of first-fruits — the origin of the saying 'Fear a returning arrow'. His funeral, with geese, sparrows and wrens as bearers, pounders and mourners, is the prototype of Japanese dirges, until his look-alike friend, mistaken for the corpse, cuts down the mortuary house in anger, which falls to earth as Mount Moyama.
summary.zh: 高皇產靈尊欲平定葦原中國,先遣天穗日命,三年不報;復遣其子,亦然。乃遣天稚彥,賜天鹿兒弓與天羽羽矢。天稚彥至而下照姬為妻,八年不報。高皇產靈尊遣雉名鳴往察之;天稚彥聞築紫巫女之言,取神弓射之,雉死而矢貫胸達於天;高皇產靈尊擲矢還,中天稚彥胸,即死。是為'忌還矢'之諺。後其友阿遲鍬高日子根神弔喪,貌酷肖死者,家人誤認,怒而以大葉刈劍斬喪屋,喪屋墮地成美濃甕山,故喪歌起焉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Taka-mi-musubi desired to send his august grandchild Ninigi to rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains; but that land swarmed with deities shining like fireflies and buzzing like flies, and its very trees and herbs could speak. So he assembled the eighty gods and asked whom he should send to expel and subdue the evil ones. All recommended Ame-no-ho-hi, the most heroic among the gods; but he curried favour with Oho-na-mochi and for three years made no report. His son Oho-se-ihi, sent after him, yielded compliance to his father and likewise never reported. The gods then advised sending Ame-waka-hiko, son of Ame no kuni-dama, a valorous person; Taka-mi-musubi gave him a heavenly deer-bow and heavenly feathered arrows and despatched him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §1–2 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ame-waka-hiko, however, was disloyal: as soon as he arrived he took to wife Shita-teru-hime, daughter of Utsushi-kuni-dama, remained, and declared that he too wished to govern the Central Land of Reed-Plains. He never reported the result of his mission. At last, wondering why he was so long silent, Taka-mi-musubi sent the pheasant Na-naki to observe; the bird flew down and perched on a many-branched cassia-tree before his gate. Ama-no-sagu-me told Ame-waka-hiko that a strange bird sat there; he took the heavenly bow and arrows given him by Taka-mi-musubi and shot the pheasant so that it died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §2 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The arrow passed through the pheasant's breast and came before Taka-mi-musubi where he sat. He saw that it was stained with blood, surmised it had been fighting the earthly deities, took it up and flung it back down to earth; falling, it struck Ame-waka-hiko on the top of his breast as he lay resting after the feast of first-fruits, and he died immediately. This was the origin of the saying, 'Fear a returning arrow.' In one variant it is Amaterasu herself who sends Ame-waka-hiko; he marries many daughters of the earthly deities, and for eight years sends no report; when she flings the arrow back she pronounces a curse over it, that if it was shot with evil intent mischief should surely come upon him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §2–3 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sound of his wife's weeping reached heaven; his father Ame no kuni-dama sent down a swift wind to bring the body up, and a mortuary house was built. The river-geese were made head-hanging bearers and broom-bearers; in one version the barn-door fowls were head-hanging bearers, the kingfisher the representative of the deceased, the sparrows the pounding-women, and the wrens the mourners; for eight days and eight nights they wept and sang dirges — the origin of the Japanese funeral lament. Then his friend Aji-suki-taka-hiko-ne ascended to condole, being exactly like Ame-waka-hiko in appearance. The parents, relations, wife and children cried that their lord was still alive and clung to his garments; flushed with anger, he drew his sword Oho-ha-kari and cut down the mortuary house, which fell to earth and became a mountain, Moyama, mourning mountain, in the province of Mino. This is why people take care not to mistake a living man for a dead one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §4–5 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: Take-mika-dzuchi Subdues Izumo — the Kuni-yuzuri
title.zh: 日本書紀·建御雷神平定葦原中國

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: To prepare the descent of the August Grandchild, heaven despatches Futsu-nushi and Take-mika-dzuchi to demand the surrender of the Central Land of Reed-Plains. They draw their swords, stick them point-down in the earth, and sit on the points to question Okuninushi, whose son Kotoshironushi — consulted while angling at Cape Miho — counsels submission. Okuninushi hands over the broad spear he used to pacify the land, introduces Kunado as his deputy, and withdraws to concealment; the envoys then put to death all the rebellious spirits, the last hold-out being the star-god Kagase-wo. Rival writings make the negotiation twice refused, then bought with a promise of palaces, rice-fields and a heavenly bride, Miho-tsu-hime.
summary.zh: 天孫將降,高皇產靈尊乃遣經津主神與建御雷神往定葦原中國。二神至出雲伊那佐小濱,拔十拳劍倒插於地,坐其鋒而問大己貴神。大己貴神使使往問其子事代主神——時方於美穗岬釣魚;事代主神答以當奉還,乃以青枝垣八重圍之而去。大己貴神遂以其平國所用之大刀奉上,自隱於根國。二神誅滅惡神,星神香具背男獨不伏,遣織女武葉槌神乃服。一書則載大己貴神初拒之,天神許以宮殿田疇、高天原之女彌都久姬為妻,乃讓國,以事代主神代掌其事而隱去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); the kuni-yuzuri is the mythic charter of imperial rule; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Taka-mi-musubi again assembled all the gods to choose one to send to the Central Land of Reed-Plains. All said it would be well to send Futsu-nushi, son of Iha-tsutsu no wo and Iha-tsutsu no me. But certain gods dwelt in the Rock Cave of Heaven, among them Mika no Haya-hi, his son Hi no Haya-hi, and the latter's son Take-mika-dzuchi; the last came forward indignantly: was Futsu-nushi alone to be reckoned a hero? Was he not a hero too? He was therefore associated with Futsu-nushi and sent to subdue the Central Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §6–7 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two gods descended to the Little Shore of Itasa in Izumo, drew their ten-span swords, stuck them upside down in the earth, and, sitting on their points, questioned Oho-na-mochi: Taka-mi-musubi wished to send down his August Grandchild to preside over this country as its lord, and had sent them to clear out and pacify it — would he stand aside or no? Oho-na-mochi answered that he must ask his son before replying. Koto-shiro-nushi was away on an excursion, angling for fish at Cape Miho — some say catching birds — in the many-handed boat of Kumano; a messenger, Inase-hagi, was sent to him by boat, and he answered that the Heavenly Deity had addressed them the inquiry, that his father ought respectfully to withdraw, and that he would make no opposition. So he made an eight-fold fence of green branches in the sea, stepped on the bow of his boat, and went off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §7–8 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oho-na-mochi then spoke to the two gods in accordance with his son's words: his son, on whom he relied, had already departed, and he too would depart; if he made resistance, all the gods of the land would resist likewise. He took the broad spear which he had used as a staff when pacifying the land and gave it to them: by means of this spear he had been successful, and if the Heavenly Grandchild used it to rule the land he would undoubtedly subdue it to tranquillity. So he withdrew to the concealment of the hundred-and-eighty road-windings and became concealed. The two gods then put to death all the rebellious spirits and deities; the only one who refused submission was the star-god Kagase-wo, who yielded when the Weaver-God Take-ha-dzuchi was sent against him, and the two gods ascended to heaven and reported their success.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §8–9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: A fuller variant makes the negotiation harder. When Futsu-nushi and Take-mika-dzuchi first asked whether he would deliver up the country, Oho-na-mochi answered that he had suspected they were coming to his place, and would not allow it. Futsu-nushi returned and reported; Taka-mi-musubi sent them back with generous instructions: let the public matters be conducted by his grandchild, while Okuninushi ruled divine affairs — heaven would build him the palace of Ama-no-Hi-sumi, with high massy pillars and broad thick planks, cultivate his rice-fields, make him a high bridge, a floating bridge and a heavenly bird-boat for his sea-pleasures, white shields of one hundred and eighty seams, and appoint Ame-no-ho-hi president of the festivals in his honour. Okuninushi yielded: let the August Grandchild direct the public affairs, and he would retire to direct secret matters; he introduced Kunado as his deputy, invested him with the pure Yasaka jewels, became concealed for ever, and Taka-mi-musubi gave him her daughter Miho-tsu-hime to wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §12–13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: The Descent of the August Grandchild Ninigi
title.zh: 日本書紀·天孫瓊瓊杵尊降臨

region.en: Peak of Takachiho, Hiuga (modern Takachiho plateau, Miyazaki)
region.zh: 日向高千穗峰(今宮崎縣高千穗)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Taka-mi-musubi casts the coverlet of the true couch over the August Grandchild Ama-tsu-hiko-hiko-ho-no-ninigi and sends him down through the eight-fold clouds of heaven to the Peak of Takachiho in Hiuga. Amaterasu bestows the three treasures — the curved jewel, the eight-hand mirror and the sword Kusanagi — with five attendant gods of the first Be corporations, entrusts him with the rice-ears of the sacred garden, and consecrates the mirror with the prayer that looking on it be as looking on her. The road-god Saruta-hiko, seven hands in the nose and glowing from mouth and posteriors, meets them at the crossways, is questioned by the unabashed Uzume, and becomes the Grandchild's harbinger to Ise.
summary.zh: 高皇產靈尊以真床覆衾裹瓊瓊杵尊,令其闢天磐座,杝八重雲而降於日向高千穗之峰。天照大神授三種神器——八尺瓊勾玉、八咫鏡、草薙劍——并以天兒屋命、布刀玉命、天鈿女命、石凝姥命、玉屋命五部神為屬;又授齋庭稻穗,囑其子孫永為葦原千五百秋之主。天兒屋命奉鏡祝辭:見此鏡當如見吾。時猿田毘古大神候於天八衢,鼻長七手,背高七尺,口尻皆有光;天鈿女命袒胸而問之,猿田毘古乃為前導,將赴伊勢五十鈴川上流。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); the descent of the imperial ancestor is the charter myth of Japanese sacred kingship; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Taka-mi-musubi took the coverlet which was on his true couch, cast it over his August Grandchild Ama-tsu-hiko-hiko-ho-ninigi, and made him descend. The August Grandchild left his heavenly rock-seat, clove his way with an awful path-cleaving through the eight-fold clouds of heaven, and descended on the Peak of Takachiho of So in Hiuga. He took his stand on a level part of the floating sand-bank, traversed the desert land of Sojishi from the Hill of Hitawo in search of a country, and came to Cape Kasasa in Ata-no-nagaya, where a man of that land, Koto-katsu-kuni-katsu Nagasa, told him there was a country and begged him to roam through it at his pleasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §9 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu gave the August Grandchild the three treasures, the curved jewel of Yasaka gem, the eight-hand mirror, and the sword Kusanagi, joining to him as attendants Ame no Koyane, first ancestor of the Nakatomi; Futo-dama, first ancestor of the Imibe; Ame no Uzume, first ancestor of the Sarume; Ishi-kori-dome, first ancestor of the mirror-makers; and Tamaya, first ancestor of the jewel-makers — gods of five Be. She commanded him: this Reed-plain-1500-autumns fair-rice-ear Land is the region which her descendants should be lords of; let him proceed thither and govern it, and may his dynasty, like heaven and earth, endure for ever. She also gave over to him the rice-ears of the sacred garden of which she partook in the Plain of High Heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §11–12 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Amaterasu took the precious mirror in her hand, gave it to Ame no Oshi-ho-mimi and uttered a prayer: my child, when thou lookest upon this mirror, let it be as if thou wert looking on me; let it be with thee on thy couch and in thy hall, a holy mirror. The Koyane and Futo-dama were commanded to guard it well. At the descent itself, one sent in advance returned and reported that at the eight-cross-roads of heaven dwelt a god the length of whose nose was seven hands and of whose back more than seven fathoms, with light shining from his mouth and posteriors, and eyeballs like an eight-hand mirror with a ruddy glow like the winter-cherry. None of the eighty-myriad deities dared confront him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §12–13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Uzume was specially commanded to question him, being superior in the power of her looks. She bared her breasts, pushed the band of her garment down below her navel, and confronted him with a mocking laugh. The god of the crossways asked what this behaviour meant; she replied by asking who he was to remain in the road by which the child of Amaterasu was to make his progress. He answered: hearing that the child of Amaterasu was about to descend, he had come respectfully to meet and attend upon him — his name was Saruta-hiko. Asked whether he would go before or she, he chose to go before and be the harbinger, directing the Grandchild to the Peak of Kushifuru of Takachiho and himself to the upper waters of the River Isuzu at Sanada in Ise. Uzume attended him, and for having discovered him received the designation Sarume no Kimi, from which the male and female Lords of Sarume were both styled Kimi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §13 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.zh: 日本書紀·木花咲耶姬火中產子

region.en: Cape Kasasa, Ata, in Hiuga (modern Kagoshima, Kyushu)
region.zh: 日向國阿多之笠沙岬(今鹿兒島)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: At Cape Kasasa the August Grandchild Ninigi meets the fair maiden Konohana-sakuya, daughter of the mountain god Oho-yama-tsu-mi, and weds her after rejecting her elder sister Iha-naga — who curses the race of man to brief lives like the flowers of the trees. When Konohana conceives in one night, Ninigi doubts the child is his; she builds a doorless parturition hut, swears an ordeal by fire, sets it alight, and from the flames are born her three or four sons unharmed — including Hiko-hoho-demi, ancestor of the emperors.
summary.zh: 瓊瓊杵尊至笠沙岬,遇大山祇神之女木花咲耶姬,娶之;嫌其姊石長姬醜而退之,石長姬羞憤咒曰:若取吾則子孫壽如磐石,今唯娶妹,帝祚當如木花之易謝——此人命所以短也。木花咲耶姬一夜有孕,瓊瓊杵尊疑非己子;姬立無戶之產室,誓曰:若所懷非天孫之胤,願焚死;遂入室自焚,火中先後生火須勢理命、火明命、彥火火出見尊,母子皆無恙。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After his descent the August Grandchild erected a palace-hall at Cape Kasasa, and walking afterwards by the sea-shore saw a beautiful woman, Kami-ataka-ashi-tsu-hime, also called Ko-no-hana-saku-ya-hime, daughter of the mountain god Oho-yama-tsu-mi. He asked her in marriage; her father sent his two daughters with a hundred tables of food and drink. The Grandchild thought the elder sister Iha-naga ugly and would not take her, but took the noted younger sister, who conceived in one night. Iha-naga was greatly ashamed and cursed him: had he taken her, the children born to him would have been long-lived, enduring like the massy rocks; but since he had married her sister only, the children born to him would be decadent like the flowers of the trees — and in one version she spat and wept that the race of visible mankind should change swiftly like the flowers of the trees and decay and pass away. This is the reason why the life of man is so short.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §14–15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Konohana-sakuya announced her pregnancy; the August Grandchild declared that though he was a heavenly deity, how could he cause any one to become with child in one night, and that the child in her bosom was assuredly not his. Wroth and ashamed, she made a doorless muro, a parturition-hut, and made a vow: if the child she had conceived were the offspring of another deity, might it assuredly be destroyed; but if it were truly the offspring of the Heavenly Grandchild, might it surely live unharmed. Then she entered the muro and set it on fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §15 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the flames first broke out, a child was born who was named Ho-no-susori; when the flame reached its height, a child was born named Ho-no-akari; and the next child born was Hiko-hoho-demi — three children in all, the fire failing to harm them and the mother unharmed. A variant writing has four sons who announce themselves from the fire, one at the first brightness, one at its height, one when the flames were becoming extinguished, and one as she recoiled from the heat; the mother came forth from the embers unscathed, and the Grandchild confessed that his mockery had been deliberate, to let every one know that a heavenly deity can cause pregnancy in one night. From the bamboo knife with which she cut their navel-strings there eventually sprang up a bamboo grove, and the place was called Takaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §15–16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Konohana-sakuya, by divination, fixed upon a rice-field which she named Sanada, and from the rice grown there brewed heavenly sweet sake with which she entertained the Grandchild — the mythic counterpart of the annual Nihi-name festival of first-fruits. A long time after, the August Grandchild died and was buried in the Misasagi of Hiuga-no-ye in Tsukushi, closing the story of the divine ancestor's earthly career.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §16 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi: Hohodemi and the Lost Fish-Hook at the Sea-God's Palace
title.zh: 日本書紀·彥火火出見失鉤與海神宮

region.en: Sea-palace of the Sea-God Toyotama-hiko (symbolic pin on the Hiuga coast, Kyushu)
region.zh: 海神豐玉毘古之宮(象徵定位:日向海岸)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: Hiko-hoho-demi, who has a mountain-gift, trades talents with his sea-gifted elder brother Ho-no-susori and loses his brother's fish-hook. Grieving on the shore, he is sunk in a basket-boat to the Sea-God's crenellated palace, where he marries the Sea-God's daughter Toyotama-hime and lives three years; the lost hook is recovered from the mouth of the red tai, and the Sea-God sends him home with the tide-flowing and tide-ebbing jewels. With them he drowns and humbles his brother, whose descendants become the Hayato mimes of the imperial court.
summary.zh: 火須勢理命有海幸,彥火火出見尊有山幸;二兄易其利器,俱不得利。弟失兄之釣鉤,造新鉤數千不獲允;海濱悲泣,遇鹽椎老翁,編竹籃沉之海底,至海神之宮。綿津見神款待之,以女豐玉毘賣妻焉;三年後欲歸,海神於赤女(鯛)口中得鉤,授以潮滿珠、潮涸珠,教以咒鉤之辭。弟歸,以潮滿珠溺其兄,兄乃稱臣為俳優,子孫世為隼人,侍於皇宮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The elder brother Ho-no-susori had by nature a sea-gift, and the younger brother Hiko-hoho-demi a mountain-gift. They exchanged gifts for trial, but neither gained aught by it. The elder repented and demanded his fish-hook back; the younger had already lost it, made another, then forged thousands from his cross-sword and heaped them in a winnowing tray — all refused. His grief was profound; he went and made moan by the shore of the sea, where he met Shiho-tsutsu no Oji. The old man made a basket without interstices, placed him in it, and sank it in the sea. Hohodemi found himself at a pleasant strand and arrived suddenly at the palace of the Sea-God, provided with battlements and turrets and stately towers, with a well before the gate over which grew a many-branched cassia-tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §29 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: A beautiful woman came out from within, took a jewel-vessel, and was about to draw water when, raising her eyes, she saw him and was alarmed, returning to tell her father and mother of the rare stranger at the foot of the tree. The Sea-God prepared an eight-fold cushion and led him in, and heard all the circumstances from first to last. He assembled the fishes, both great and small, and required an answer of them; all knew not, only the Red-woman (the red tai) had had a sore mouth for some time past. She was summoned peremptorily, her mouth examined, and the lost hook was found. Then Hohodemi took the Sea-God's daughter Toyotama-hime to wife and dwelt in the sea-palace; for three years he enjoyed peace and pleasure, but still longed for his own country and sighed deeply from time to time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §30–31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sea-God returned the hook with instructions: when giving it to the elder brother, first call to it secretly 'a poor hook', or in one version recite 'the origin of poverty, the beginning of starvation, the root of wretchedness', and in another spit thrice; and if the brother should cross the sea, the Sea-God would stir up the blasts and billows to overwhelm him. He gave also the jewel of the flowing tide and the jewel of the ebbing tide: dip the first and the tide shall drown the brother; dip the second and the tide shall ebb and save him — by harassing him thus the elder brother would of his own accord render submission. One writing adds advice about fields: if the elder brother makes high fields, the younger should make puddle fields, and conversely, so that the Sea-God might in all sincerity lend his aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §31 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Back in his own palace, Hohodemi followed the god's instructions. The elder brother, in the utmost straits, of his own accord admitted his offence: henceforward he would be his subject to perform mimic dances — spare my life. In the fuller variant he is drowned thrice: the tide-flowing jewel submerges field, plain and mountain, and at the last he climbs a lofty tree and cries that his descendants for eighty generations shall serve as mimes in ordinary — one version has dog-men. In another, the younger brother stands on the sea-shore and whistles; a sudden tempest overwhelms the fishing fleet, and the elder brother, with nothing but his waistcloth, smears his face and palms with red earth, and, kicking up his feet, practises the manner of his drowning struggles: foot-divination when the tide reaches his feet, raised feet at his knees, circling at his thighs, hands on his breast, thrown-up hands at his neck. From that time until now this custom has never ceased, and the Hayato who guard the imperial palace serve instead of barking dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §32–34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

title.en: Nihongi Variant: Toyotama-hime's Childbirth by the Sea
title.zh: 日本書紀異傳·豐玉毘賣臨海產子

region.en: Parturition-house on the shore of Hiuga (modern Miyazaki coast)

source.work: Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697, Vol. I, trans. W. G. Aston (1896)

summary.en: The sea-born bride Toyotama-hime promises to come ashore in raging winds and waves, and begs Hohodemi to build her a parturition-house and not look upon her in travail. Unable to restrain himself, he peers in and sees her changed into a great sea-monster of eight fathoms; in shame she abandons the newborn, bars the sea-path, and departs — forfeiting the friendship between sea and land. The child, born before the cormorant-feather thatch was finished, is named Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu, and is reared by his aunt Tama-yori-hime, whom he later marries: their sons include Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, the future Emperor Jimmu.
summary.zh: 豐玉毘賣自誓:當以怒風怒浪之日來產,請造產室相待,臨蓐勿窺。彥火火出見尊不能忍,竊自窺之,則見其化為八尋大鰐,方蟠委而產。妃大慚,曰:本欲使海陸相通,永不睽隔;今既見辱,何以親睦?乃以葦纏兒置之渚,塞海途而返。兒因產室以鸕羽葺之未竟而生,名曰彥波瀲武鸕鶿草葺不合尊。後玉依毘賣育之,尊娶姨為妃,生四子,季子神日本磐余彥,即神武天皇之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Nihongi, Book II); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Hohodemi was about to return home, Toyotama-hime addressed him: thy handmaiden is already pregnant, and the time of her delivery is not far off; on a day when the winds and waves are raging, I will surely come forth to the sea-shore, and I pray thee make for me a parturition-house and await me there. She fulfilled her promise, bringing with her her younger sister Tama-yori-hime, and bravely confronting the winds and waves came to the sea-shore. When the time of her delivery was at hand she besought him: when thy handmaiden is in travail, do not look upon her. The Heavenly Grandchild could not restrain himself, but went secretly and peeped in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §33–34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Toyotama-hime was just in childbirth, and had changed into a dragon — in another telling, into an enormous sea-monster of eight fathoms, wriggling about on her belly. Greatly ashamed, she said: hadst thou not disgraced me, I would have made the sea and land communicate with each other, and for ever prevented them from being sundered; but now that thou hast disgraced me, wherewithal shall friendly feelings be knit together? So she wrapped the infant in rushes and abandoned it on the sea-shore; then she barred the sea-path and passed away. Accordingly the child was called Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu — because in one version the parturition-house by the sea-shore was thatched with cormorants' feathers and the child was born before the tiles had met.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §34 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Variant writings supply the name more fully. In one, Hohodemi built the parturition-house of cormorants' feathers for thatch, and Toyotama-hime arrived riding on a great tortoise with her younger sister Tama-yori-hime, throwing a splendour over the sea; her months were already fulfilled, so she entered before the thatching was completed. Asked by what name the child ought to be called, she answered Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu and departed straight across the sea. Another account has her withhold the child at first out of resentment, then send it back with Tama-yori-hime, having taken the coverlet of the true couch and rushes to wrap him in — and for this reason, it is said, there is no communication between land and sea. She later sent the verse of poetry of the island of wild-ducks, regretting the parting; the provisioning of wet-nurses, boiled-rice-chewers and washerwomen for the infant is given as the origin of the practice of engaging wet-nurses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §34–36 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahezu took his aunt Tama-yori-hime as his consort, and had by her four male children: Hiko-itsu-se, Ina-ihi, Mi-ke-iri-no, and Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko — the youngest variously styled Sano in childhood, and, after he had cleared and subdued the realm, honoured with the title by which he is known as the first emperor. Long after, Hiko-nagisa died in the palace of the western country and was buried in the Misasagi on the top of Mount Ahira in Hiuga; his father Hohodemi before him had been buried on the summit of Mount Takaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nihongi, Book II §38–39 (trans. Aston 1896); not verbatim.
